planting.note: Plant rhizome divisions in spring or fall in humus-rich, well-drained woodland soil in partial to full shade; this compact Central Asian species stays low and is well suited to a shaded rock garden or trough rather than a border.

directions: Pink Solomon's seal is a diminutive species native to the mountains of Xinjiang, Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, and Tajikistan, where it grows in rocky, humus-rich ground far shorter than the familiar arching border Solomon's seals. In mid-spring it carries small, pale-to-deep-pink bells in pairs from the leaf axils along short, upright stems, followed in autumn by whorls of red berries. Plant divisions in humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade, and give it a spot among rocks or low companions where its compact habit will not be swamped by taller neighbors. It is slower-spreading than common garden Polygonatum species, making it a good choice for a shaded rock garden or container rather than a groundcover role.
sources: Plants of the World Online (Kew Science)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container stock in spring in humus-rich, well-drained soil in light to full shade; established colonies tolerate drier shade better than many eastern wild gingers.

directions: This Japanese woodland species is unusual among wild gingers for bearing its small, rosy-pink, strongly reflexed flowers on a short visible stem above the rootstock rather than tucked flush against the ground. Deep green, heart-shaped leaves with deeply impressed veins clothe slowly spreading, stoloniferous rhizomes, forming an evergreen-to-semi-evergreen patch over time. Plant divisions in humus-rich, well-drained soil in light to full shade; it is considered one of the easier Asian gingers to grow and tolerates drier summer shade once established better than many of its eastern North American relatives.

planting.note: Plant divisions or container stock in spring in humus-rich, moist, well-drained soil in light to full shade; this Taiwanese species thrives in hot, humid summer climates better than many cold-hardy wild gingers.

directions: Native to the hill forests of Taiwan, this creeping evergreen wild ginger forms a low mat of glossy, triangular leaves patterned with silvery veining. In early spring it produces ruffled, purple-and-silver mottled flowers tucked beneath the foliage at ground level. Plant in humus-rich, consistently moist, well-drained soil in light to full shade; it has proven notably tolerant of hot, humid summer conditions, performing better in the warm-summer Southeast than many other evergreen Asian Asarum species.
sources: Plants of the World Online (Kew Science)

planting.note: Divide established plants in spring and set into consistently moist, humus-rich soil in a cool-summer montane climate; this species is restricted to the high mountains of the Four Corners region and does not tolerate hot, dry lowland summers.

directions: Saffron ragwort is a Rocky Mountain native restricted to a small range centered on Colorado, Wyoming, Montana, Utah, and New Mexico, where it grows in moist, densely vegetated subalpine and montane meadows. Unlike the yellow-flowered Packera species common in gardens, it is prized for its unusual rich orange-to-red buds opening to orange and yellow flowers through the summer. It needs consistently moist, humus-rich soil and the cool summer nights of a high-elevation climate, making it a specialty plant for cold-climate native and bog gardens rather than general landscape use.

planting.note: Divide established plants in spring and set into cool, consistently moist, gravelly or rocky soil in partial shade to sun; this northern species needs a cold climate and does not tolerate hot summers.

directions: Rayless mountain ragwort ranges across cold northern habitats from Alaska and the western Rockies to the Great Lakes region and eastern Canada, occurring in moist rocky or gravelly ground along stream banks, lakeshores, and bogs. Its yellow disk flowers are arranged in a candelabra-like cluster and typically lack ray petals, though occasional plants show a few short rays, a quirky trait that distinguishes it from showier garden Packera species. Plant divisions in cool, consistently moist, humus- or mineral-rich soil in partial shade to sun, and expect it to thrive only where summers stay cool, as in bog gardens or cold-climate native plantings near its natural range.
